newsitem.title: USA: Disney says Fla. community is not a hobby.
newsitem.headline: Disney says Fla. community is not a hobby.

text.p: Officials of Walt Disney Co will not reveal how much the company is investing in Celebration, a planned community of homes and businesses under development in Florida, but they insist the project makes economic sense.

"A popular myth is that we're doing this as a hobby, or that there's some reason to do it other than for business," said Peter Rummell, head of Disney's Imagineering unit. He commented on Wednesday after a tour of the project for architects and journalists.
Celebration is one of Disney's most unusual projects in that it is designed for year-round residents, not to entertain tourists.
Disney has spent billions of dollars to build resorts, theme parks, shops and restaurants in the sprawling Walt Disney World development since it opened 25 years ago.

"This is a business, just like anything else we do is a business. I assure you it has gotten the same rigor that anything else we do has. It makes very nice economic sense for us," he added. "It is a prudent investment for us."
Rummell and Disney chief Michael Eisner declined to say how much Disney has invested in Celebration, or when they expected the project to show a profit.
Disney's investment in Celebration has been estimated in the hundreds of millions of dollars by some entertainment experts.

Wall Street analysts, invited to Disney World's 25th anniversary party this week, were told that the company estimates spending about $1 billion on its new Animal Kingdom theme park, about $100 million on its Disney Wide World of Sports complex and more than $50 million for the General Motors Test Track ride. All are currently in construction in Florida.
By contrast, Disney has never estimated spending on Celebration.

It has attracted attention among architects and urban planners. World-reknown architects Cesar Pelli, Aldo Rossi, Philip Johnson and others have designed office and municipal buildings within walking distance of old-fashioned homes with porches, alleys and white picket fences.
The project is also unusual in that it includes a hospital and public school, both planned as central components of the town.

The first few dozen families moved into Celebration this autumn, and construction of the first phase is continuing at a rapid pace. Eventually, the town is expected to have 8,000 homes ranging in price from $130,000 for a townhouse to nearly $1 million for custom-designed estates.

Disney has been criticized by some for its strict rules and deed restrictions governing purchases of Celebration homes. For example, some rules forbid reselling a home for at least three years, and force buyers to choose from among a half-dozen architectural styles.
The rules are intended to "help the community get off to a good start," Rummell said. "You can either buy into it or go somewhere else."
